heroImage.alt: Dr. Patricia Langford, Board-Certified Gastroenterologist with patient before and after results

paragraphs: If you’re on Ozempic, Wegovy, or Mounjaro and your stomach feels like it’s full of cement, you can’t stop burping sulfur, and you haven’t had a normal bowel movement in weeks — I need you to hear this.
Because what I’m about to tell you is going to make you furious.

The medication that’s finally silencing your food noise is quietly wrecking your digestion from the top down. Not just “causing constipation.” Something deeper. And when you bring it up to your doctor, they’re going to tell you to take Miralax and drink more water.
There’s a reason that advice doesn’t work. I know because I’ve watched it fail from the other side of the exam room for 23 years.
But it was a 58-year-old woman named Karen who finally made me stop handing out the same useless advice and start asking why.
Five months on Wegovy. Down 31 pounds. Bloodwork beautiful. On paper, a textbook success.
Then I asked about digestive issues. She looked at the floor. Then at me. The expression I’ve seen a thousand times — someone deciding whether to tell the truth.
“I haven’t gone to the bathroom in eleven days.”

Then it all came out. Bloating so severe she couldn’t button her pants. Sulfur burps so bad her grandson commented on her breath at his baseball game — in front of the whole bleacher section. An enema she’d given herself at a gas station bathroom because the pain was a ten out of ten. A medicine cabinet full of Miralax, Dulcolax, Colace, fiber gummies, Smooth Move tea, and prune juice she hid behind the orange juice. A spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she’d gone.
Then she said the thing I hear from every one of these women:

sections.text: “But I’ve lost 31 pounds. So I just deal with it.”

paragraphs: The medication is giving her the body she’s wanted for thirty years. But she’s too sick to enjoy living in it.

The doctor spent nine minutes with her. Told her to drink more water and try Miralax. She told him she’d been taking Miralax every day for three months. He suggested Linzess or lowering her dose. She went white. “Lower my dose? I’ve lost thirty-one pounds.”
She left. At the door she turned and said, “He didn’t hear a single thing I said, did he?”
She didn’t call back. They never do. The weight is still coming off. They’ve decided the suffering is the price of admission.
Karen broke something in me. She wasn’t the first. She was just the one who made me start asking why nothing ever worked.

You already know the answer if you’ve been reading about this. GLP-1 medications slow the stomach, not the colon. Food sits for hours — sometimes days. It ferments. It dries out. By the time anything reaches the colon, it’s already a brick. The colon isn’t blocked. It’s empty. And every product in Karen’s medicine cabinet was aimed at the colon — six feet downstream from where the problem actually starts.
That’s textbook pathophysiology. I teach it. But until Karen, I’d never connected it to why I was recommending the same failed solutions my colleagues were.

sections.alt: Upstream vs downstream mechanism — GLP-1 slows the stomach but laxatives target the colon

sections.text: What Three Nights on PubMed Revealed

paragraphs: I pulled the actual research. Not patient forums. The clinical studies. And three mechanisms kept surfacing that no single product was addressing together.

First — gastric motility. A 2022 study in the World Journal of Gastroenterology showed that GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce gastric emptying by up to 40%. The vagus nerve — the nerve that tells the stomach when to push food through — gets effectively muted. The compound showing the most consistent motility support in preclinical models was apigenin, found in high concentrations in celery. Not override the medication. Restore the signal. Like turning the volume back up on a speaker someone turned down.

Second — hydrogen sulfide. Slowed motility means bacterial overgrowth. In a 2021 Gut Microbes analysis, patients on GLP-1 agonists showed a 3.2x increase in sulfate-reducing bacteria — the organisms that produce that rotten-egg gas. Chlorophyllin, a concentrated form of chlorophyll, binds directly to hydrogen sulfide and neutralizes it at the molecular level. A controlled trial showed a 74% reduction in sulfur compound odor within 14 days.

Third — downstream congestion. Even with the stomach moving again, weeks of backup means the small intestine and colon are still congested. The answer wasn’t bulk fiber — that’s the last thing a jammed system needs. It was a specific type of low-bulk, gel-forming soluble prebiotic fiber that draws moisture in and softens what’s stuck without adding volume to the gridlock.

sections.text: Three mechanisms. Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three must work together — or you’re only addressing a fraction of the problem.

paragraphs: That’s when I understood why Karen’s medicine cabinet never stood a chance. Miralax pulls water into the colon — but nothing was sitting there. Fiber adds bulk on top of a closed on-ramp. Dulcolax squeezes an empty tube. Every product addressed one piece, and most addressed the wrong piece entirely.

I searched for something that combined all three mechanisms. Found motility supplements with ginger but nothing for the gas. Chlorophyll drops with no motility support. Fiber blends that would have made everything worse.
Then I found a small company that had built a gummy specifically for GLP-1 users. Not a general digestive supplement repackaged with a new label.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyllin. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I’d been reading. Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three, at concentrations that matched the research.

I also checked what it didn’t contain. No stimulant laxatives. No bulk fiber. No magnesium at doses that cause cramping. Nothing that would interfere with the GLP-1 medication itself — I verified that before I’d recommend it to anyone. It works alongside the medication, not against it.
I ordered two bottles. One to evaluate. One for Karen.

I called Karen the next day. She’d stopped coming to our clinic — I wasn’t surprised. I told her I’d found something that worked on the stomach instead of the colon, and I thought it was worth thirty days.
“At this point I’ll try anything.”
Two gummies a day. She started the following Monday.
Day three: “Nothing yet.” I told her to give it time. This wasn’t a laxative. It wasn’t forcing anything.
Day five: “Bloating feels a little less. Maybe placebo.”
Day ten: “I went this morning. On my own. No Miralax. No enema. Just went.”
That text shouldn’t have hit as hard as it did. But it did. Because I knew about the eleven days. The gas station. The spreadsheet. The baseball game.
Week three — the sulfur burps were nearly gone. Month one — she threw out the spreadsheet. Still on Wegovy. Still losing weight. But she wasn’t paying the tax anymore.
Month two — her husband noticed she was going out again. Saying yes to dinners. Staying for the whole visit at the grandkids’ house.
“He said I seem like myself again,” she told me. “He didn’t know I’d been gone.”

What I Need You to Hear

paragraphs: Here’s what I need you to hear — from a doctor who has watched this happen over and over:

Your doctors aren’t lying when they say constipation is a common side effect. They’re right. But they’re wrong about where it starts. And because they’re wrong about where it starts, every solution they offer is aimed at the wrong place.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. That’s not a mystery. That’s mechanics. And until something addresses all three, you can take every laxative in the pharmacy and still end up on day eleven with a spreadsheet and an enema kit in your purse.
You don’t have to choose between the weight loss and your digestion. You don’t have to accept the tax.
Karen didn’t. Debra didn’t. Sandra didn’t. Linda didn’t.
And they’re all still on their medications.
